name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
answer: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms is a structured review of how artificial intelligence tools are approved, deployed, and supervised across an investment organization. It covers the full lifecycle from initial request and vendor due diligence through production use, monitoring, and retirement. The audit examines whether AI use aligns with the firm's fiduciary duties, investment mandates, and client disclosures. It also checks that staff have the training and support needed to use these tools responsibly. The scope typically includes research, trading, portfolio management, compliance, risk, and client reporting functions.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the firm's existing governance, risk, and compliance platforms, along with any AI tool registry or model inventory. It relies on data from access management systems, audit logs, vendor contracts, and change management records. Documentation such as policies, procedures, and approval memos provides the evidence base. Where available, the firm's model risk management framework and data lineage tools supply technical context. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages can serve as a reference for regulatory expectations, though the audit itself is firm specific.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a combination of interviews, control walkthroughs, and sample testing. Auditors inventory every AI tool in use, then trace each one back to an approved business case and risk assessment. They test whether human oversight, output validation, and escalation paths function as designed. Findings are mapped to internal policies and external frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The result is a scored report with remediation actions and owners.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights, risk, and provenance are central to the audit. The firm must confirm that training data, model weights, and generated outputs do not violate intellectual property or client confidentiality. It must also verify that vendors provide sufficient audit rights, breach notification, and liability terms. Provenance records show where data came from, how models were trained, and who approved each use. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, which illustrates the growing legal exposure that firms must consider when enabling AI. Fiduciary duty requires that AI driven decisions remain explainable and subject to human review.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit is moving toward continuous monitoring rather than annual point in time reviews. Regulators are increasingly expecting firms to demonstrate ongoing oversight of AI systems, not just initial approval. We can expect more standardized audit criteria and third party attestations for AI vendors. Integration with existing model risk management and operational risk programs will deepen. The audit will likely become a standing function that adapts as AI tools and regulations evolve.
